clue.text: Something leaky about the camping equipment ? Ominous

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the leaky word is wrapped round the camping gear

parts.note: something that leaks is porous, letting liquid through
a tent is the basic piece of camping equipment

explanation.surface: A camper notices the gear is letting in water and takes it as a bad sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Something portentous is full of foreboding, warning of trouble to come, which is what ominous signs do.

definitions.meaning: long infantry spears, the weapons of medieval foot soldiers
freshwater predatory fish with long snouts

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both long infantry weapons with pointed heads and long-snouted freshwater predatory fish.

clue.text: Redundant in a doomed ship of course

definitions.text: Redundant in a doomed ship of course

parts.words: Redundant in a doomed ship of course
parts.note: rats are said to desert a sinking ship, so nothing to kill them is needed there

explanation.surface: On a ship that is going down, some item is plainly surplus to need.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says rats desert a sinking ship, so on a doomed vessel any vermin killer is redundant: the rats have already gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Poison laid for vermin is pointless aboard a sinking vessel, since the vermin flee before it goes down.

clue.text: Where Suffolk villagers knew their station ?

definitions.text: Where Suffolk villagers knew their station

parts.words: Where Suffolk villagers knew their station
parts.note: a Suffolk village shares its name with a London railway terminus; station seems to mean social rank

explanation.surface: Old rural folk in Suffolk knowing their place in society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knew their station' reads as knowing one's social rank, but the village of Euston in Suffolk shares its name with a London main-line railway terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: Euston is both a village in Suffolk and one of London's main railway terminals.

parts.note: a celebratory parade greeted with paper strips thrown from office windows

explanation.definitionFit: Heroes in New York parades are welcomed by streamers of paper thrown out of office windows.

parts.note: boss here is the raised knob in the centre of a shield, not a manager

explanation.definitionFit: The round projecting stud at the centre of a shield is its boss.

clue.text: Who ditched England v. Wales of all the soccer clubs ?

parts.note: taken as written
the FA, the Football Association, is the body all English soccer clubs belong to

explanation.surface: A question about which soccer club knocked England out of a match against Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ditched' is the trap: it reads as dropped from a team, but Offa, an 8th-century king of Mercia, built Offa's Dyke, the great earthwork ditch dividing England from Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: King Offa of Mercia is credited with digging the dyke, a ditch and bank, along the English-Welsh border.

clue.text: She comes up with a negative that's conditional

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: no is a negative reply
if is the word that makes a statement conditional

explanation.surface: A woman offers a refusal hedged with conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes up' turns A NO IF, read upwards in the down light, giving a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiona is a woman's first name, so it stands for a female, 'she'.

indicators.note: smuggled goods are shifted about secretly, so these letters are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: Hetty's mother has been caught sneaking precious stones through customs.
explanation.definitionFit: Amethysts are violet quartz stones prized as jewels.

parts.note: a figure from Greek myth with a single eye in the middle of his forehead

explanation.definitionFit: The Cyclops of Greek legend was a one-eyed giant, such as Polyphemus in the Odyssey.

parts.note: the flying things held on a string are paper toys sharing a name with a bird of prey

explanation.definitionFit: Toy kites fly on a string, and the kite is also a bird of prey, so these are birds that are tied down.

parts.note: a young fox is a cub, and a den is a hole, so a little fox's den is a cub's hole

explanation.definitionFit: A small snug cupboard or nook is named as if it were a hole for a young fox.

clue.text: Oxon hill as Shavian Captain's game covert ?

definitions.meaning: ... Hill rises just east of Oxford in Oxfordshire (Oxon)
Captain ... is the old sea captain in Shaw's play Heartbreak House
a covert where game birds are hunted is ground that is ...

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: a hill near Oxford, a character from George Bernard Shaw (Shavian means of Shaw), and a covert that has been 'shot over' by guns after game birds.
explanation.definitionFit: The one name covers an Oxfordshire hill, Shaw's captain in Heartbreak House, and land where guns have fired at game.

clue.text: Reorganize the chapel on principle of branch involvement

indicators.note: to reorganize something is to arrange its parts afresh, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A church committee plans to reorganize the chapel along the lines of how its branches are involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reorganize' rearranges CHAPEL. 'branch involvement' sounds like church administration but means real tree branches woven together.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleaching is the gardening technique of interlacing the branches of trees to form a hedge or walk.

clue.text: Lincolnshire source of the Pussy-cat's ring

definitions.text: Lincolnshire source of the Pussy-cat's ring

parts.words: Lincolnshire source of the Pussy-cat's ring
parts.note: a Lincolnshire village named as if after a pig's head; Lear's Owl and the Pussy-cat bought their ring from the nose of a pig

explanation.surface: A Lincolnshire place is said to have supplied the ring in a nursery poem.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edward Lear's 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat' the ring comes from the end of the nose of a Piggy-wig, so its source is a pig's head; Swineshead is a village in Lincolnshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Swineshead is a Lincolnshire village whose name also describes a pig's head, where Lear's ring was found.

parts.note: mum means silence, and a dot is a dowry; so cash paid for keeping quiet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like a mother, but here means silent, as in 'keep mum'; 'dot' is an old word for a dowry, money handed over.
explanation.definitionFit: A bribe paid to make someone keep a secret is cash for staying silent.

parts.note: a North London area with a famous planned Garden Suburb

explanation.surface: An estate agent recommends a spot for keen suburban gardeners.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampstead Garden Suburb is a famous planned estate in north London, built as an ideal community, so its residents are literally 'suburban gardeners'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hampstead Garden Suburb in north London was founded as a model planned community.

parts.note: poach seems to mean cooking gently, or stealing; but the place is a pond where fish are kept for the table, named after a cooking method

explanation.surface: A recipe question about where to cook fish gently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poach' leads to cooking, and the answer's first half is indeed a cooking word; but a stew-pond is a fish pond where fish were kept alive until eaten, so a poacher would take them there.
explanation.definitionFit: A stew-pond is a pond for keeping fish until they are needed, so it is where a thief could take them.

clue.text: Have a care, Tom, and you've spent the lot!

definitions.text: Have a care, Tom, and you've spent the lot!

parts.words: Have a care, Tom, and you've spent the lot!
parts.note: a warning to a tomcat, which is said to have a fixed allowance of lives

explanation.surface: A friend warns a spendthrift called Tom he has used up all his money.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom is a tomcat, and a cat is proverbially given nine lives; 'care' also hints that care killed the cat, as the saying has it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cats are said to have nine lives, so a reckless tom risks using up its whole allowance.

clue.text: The main thing is to hold a pipe

definitions.text: The main thing is to hold a pipe

parts.words: The main thing is to hold a pipe
parts.note: a street fitting on the water main to which firemen attach their hose

explanation.surface: Advice that the essential thing is to grip a pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main thing' sounds like 'the essential point', but means a fitting on the water main, onto which a fire hose is coupled.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydrant is an outlet on a water main where firefighters connect their hoses.

clue.text: Polo will cost you £25 for a go

definitions.meaning: polo is played on small horses, the mounts known by that name
in British slang twenty-five pounds is called a ...

explanation.walkthrough: In British money slang a 'pony' is £25 (as a 'monkey' is £500), and polo is played on ponies; 'will cost you' and 'for a go' join them into a surface about the price of a ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A polo mount is a small horse, and British slang names a sum of twenty-five pounds after the same animal.

parts.note: a burden we carry is said to be ..., which run together gives the word for a responsibility

explanation.definitionFit: A burden or responsibility is something placed upon us that we must carry.

parts.note: a mounted soldier armed with a long spear, who might be thought to lance like a surgeon

explanation.definitionFit: A lancer is a cavalryman with a lance, and surgeons lance boils, so he sounds like a surgeon.

parts.note: lifeguards rescue people, and people holding savings certificates put money by

explanation.definitionFit: People who rescue others save them, and people who put money into savings certificates are thrifty depositors.

parts.note: a bigwig is a VIP; one who returns venom is a snake whose name begins with those initials

explanation.walkthrough: A bigwig is a VIP, and the snake's name begins with those letters; 'returned' adds the sense of a venomous person repaying spite.
explanation.definitionFit: The viper is Britain's venomous snake, the adder, and the word also means a spiteful person.

parts.note: in Botticelli's painting the goddess rides ashore on a scallop shell

explanation.walkthrough: In Botticelli's Birth of Venus the goddess comes ashore standing on a large scallop shell; escallop is an older spelling of scallop.
explanation.definitionFit: A scallop shell is the vessel on which Venus rides through the surf in Botticelli's famous painting.

definitions.meaning: taking quick short breaths, as after running
bags is old slang for trousers

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both gasps for breath and, as a noun, trousers or underwear.

parts.note: a payment system run by the Post Office, so cheques passing through it are post-dated in a new sense

explanation.surface: A bank asks whether customers will welcome cheques dated ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post-dated' means dated in the future, but here means handled by the Post Office, whose Giro money-transfer system was new when this puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: Giro was the British Post Office's bank transfer system, through which cheques were paid.

clue.text: No longer moody, dear ? (asks Dorothy of her daffy brother)

parts.note: ex- describes something that no longer is, as in an ex-wife
pensive means thoughtful in a melancholy, moody way

explanation.surface: Dorothy Wordsworth asks her brother, who wrote about daffodils, whether he has stopped brooding.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorothy is Dorothy Wordsworth; her 'daffy brother' is William, whose daffodil poem has him lying 'in vacant or in pensive mood'. That bracket is colour, not wordplay. 'dear' means costly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dear costs a lot of money, so it is costly or high-priced.

parts.note: a bee is a gathering of people, and spelling here means casting spells, so a gathering of witches

explanation.definitionFit: A gathering of witches who work spells together is a 'bee', a meeting, for spellcasting.

definitions.meaning: to cobble is to mend roughly, as a cobbler patches shoes
mending a hole in a sock by weaving thread across it

explanation.definitionFit: To mend a sock by weaving yarn across a hole is both a rough repair and filling the gap.

clue.text: Or heraldic impressions of seals these birds could give

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a seal pressed into wax leaves an image of the family crest

explanation.surface: Wax seals might show heraldic designs, the clue suggests, made by these birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like the conjunction but is the heraldic tincture gold. The goldcrest is a tiny British songbird with a yellow crown stripe.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldcrests are tiny songbirds, the smallest birds in Britain, named for their golden crown.
